#  3.3 Multi-Step Equations with Distribution {.unnumbered}

So far in this unit, we’ve solved one-step and two-step {{< glink equations >}}. Now some equations look “messy” because they have parentheses or several terms that belong together. The key idea in this lesson is:

Simplify first, then solve.

We’ll use a short recipe:

Use the {{< glink distributive property >}} to remove parentheses.

{{< glink combine like terms >}} on the same side.

{{< glink simplify >}} to a one- or two-step equation and solve.

Check your answer by substituting it into the original equation.

In this lesson, variables will stay on one side of the equation. Later, we’ll handle equations with variables on both sides.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I can apply the distributive property to simplify equations
- [ ] I can combine like terms before solving
- [ ] I can solve multi-step equations with multiple operations
- [ ] I can check my solutions to multi-step equations by substitution
:::

:::{.vocab}
{{< glink combine like terms >}}, {{< glink distributive property >}}, {{< glink equation >}}, {{< glink simplify >}}
:::

{{< warmup >}}

1. Solve $3x - 5 = 19$

2. Simplify $-2(3x - 4) + 2x$

3. Is $x=10$ a solution to $5(x - 1) = 45$?

{{< learn >}}

### 3.3.1 – Distribution in Equations

Sometimes equations have parentheses. When that happens, you can’t get the variable by itself right away—you have to **simplify first**. This is where the **distributive property** comes in.

Remember from Lesson 2.4:

$$
a(b + c) = ab + ac
$$

That rule lets us “remove” parentheses so the equation is easier to work with.

---

**Example 1:**

Solve:

$$
3(x + 4) = 21
$$

The variable $x$ is trapped inside the parentheses. We start by applying the distributive property to free $x$.

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{3}(x + 4) &= 21  \\
3x + 12 &= 21 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 3}}}
\end{align*}
$$

Now we can solve the two-step equation.

$$
\begin{align*}
3x + 12 \textcolor{red}{- 12} &= 21 \textcolor{red}{- 12} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{–12 both sides}}} \\
3x &= 9 \\
\\
3x \textcolor{red}{\div 3} &= 9 \textcolor{red}{\div 3} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷3 both sides}}} \\
x &= 3
\end{align*}
$$

---

**Example 2:**

Solve:

$$
-2(2x - 5) = 6
$$

Notice the negative sign. We need to be extra careful to include it when we distribute.

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{-2}(2x - 5) &= 6 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the -2}}} \\
-4x + 10 &= 6  \\
\\
-4x + 10 \textcolor{red}{- 10} &= 6 \textcolor{red}{- 10} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-10 both sides}}} \\
-4x &= -4 \\
\\
-4x \textcolor{red}{\div -4} &= -4 \textcolor{red}{\div -4} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷-4 both sides}}} \\
x &= 1
\end{align*}
$$

---

:::{.you-try title="Solve $3(2x + 1) = 15$"}
Solve:

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{3}(2x + 1) &= 15 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 3}}} \\
6x + 3 &= 15 \\
\\
6x + 3 \textcolor{red}{-3} &= 15 \textcolor{red}{-3} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-3 both sides}}}\\
6x &= 12 \\
\\
6x \textcolor{red}{\div 6} &= 12 \textcolor{red}{\div 6} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷6 both sides}}}\\
x &= 2
\end{align*}
$$

:::

---

### 3.3.2 – Combining Like Terms in Equations

Sometimes an equation looks messy because there are {{< glink like terms >}} on the same side of the equals sign. Before you can solve, you need to combine them into a single term.

---

**Example 1:**

Solve:

$$
4x + 7 + 2x = 31
$$

Start by combining the like terms $4x$ and $2x$.

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{blue}{4x} + 7 + \textcolor{blue}{2x} &= 31 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{6x} + 7 &= 31 
\end{align*}
$$

Now solve the two-step equation.

$$
\begin{align*}
6x + 7 \textcolor{red}{- 7} &= 31 \textcolor{red}{- 7} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{–7 both sides}}} \\
6x &= 24 \\
\\
6x \textcolor{red}{\div 6} &= 24 \textcolor{red}{\div 6} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷6 both sides}}} \\
x &= 4
\end{align*}
$$

---

**Example 2:**

Solve:

$$
2(x + 5) + 3x = 25
$$

This equation has both parentheses **and** like terms. Start by distributing.

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{2}(x + 5) + 3x &= 25 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 2}}} \\
2x + 10 + 3x &= 25 
\end{align*}
$$

Now combine $2x$ and $3x$.

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{blue}{2x} + 10 + \textcolor{blue}{3x} &= 25 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{5x} + 10 &= 25
\end{align*}
$$

Finish solving:

$$
\begin{align*}
5x + 10 \textcolor{red}{- 10} &= 25 \textcolor{red}{- 10} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{–10 both sides}}} \\
5x &= 15 \\
\\
5x \textcolor{red}{\div 5} &= 15 \textcolor{red}{\div 5} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷5 both sides}}} \\
x &= 3
\end{align*}
$$

---

**Example 3:**

Solve:

$$
-3(x - 4) + 2x  - 3 = 7
$$

Be careful with those negative signs!

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{-3}(x - 4) + 2x - 3 &= 7 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the -3}}} \\
-3x + 12 + 2x - 3 &= 7 \\
\\
\textcolor{blue}{-3x} + \textcolor{green}{12} + \textcolor{blue}{2x} \textcolor{green}{- 3} &= 7 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{-x} + \textcolor{green}{9} &= 7 \\
\\
-x + 9 \textcolor{red}{-9} &= 7 \textcolor{red}{- 9} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-9 both sides}}} \\
-x &= -2 \\
\\
-x \textcolor{red}{\div -1} &= -2 \textcolor{red}{\div -1} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷-1 both sides}}} \\
x &= 2
\end{align*}
$$


:::{.you-try title="Solve $4(x + 2) - 3x + 5 = 18$"}

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{4}(x + 2) - 3x + 5 &= 18 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 4}}} \\
4x + 8 - 3x + 5 &= 18 \\
\\
\textcolor{blue}{4x} + \textcolor{green}{8} + \textcolor{blue}{-3x} + \textcolor{green}{5} &= 18 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{x} + \textcolor{green}{13} &= 18 \\
\\
x + 13 \textcolor{red}{-13} &= 18 \textcolor{red}{-13} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-13 both sides}}} \\
x &= 5
\end{align*}
$$

:::

---

### 3.3.3 – Checking Your Work

As always, it is a good idea to check your answer by substituting the solution into the original equation.

---

**Example:**

Solve and check:

$$
4(x + 1) - 2x + 3 = 13
$$

**Step 1. Solve the equation**

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{4}(x + 1) - 2x + 3 &= 13 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 4}}} \\
4x + 4 - 2x + 3 &= 13 \\
\\
\textcolor{blue}{4x} + \textcolor{green}{4} + \textcolor{blue}{-2x} + \textcolor{green}{3} &= 13 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{2x} + \textcolor{green}{7} &= 13 \\
\\
2x + 7 \textcolor{red}{- 7} &= 13 \textcolor{red}{- 7} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-7 both sides}}} \\
2x &= 6 \\
\\
2x \textcolor{red}{\div 2} &= 6 \textcolor{red}{\div 2} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷2 both sides}}} \\
x &= 3
\end{align*}
$$

---

**Step 2. Check the solution**

Substitute $x = 3$ into the **original equation**:

$$
4(x + 1) - 2x + 3 = 13
$$

$$
4(\textcolor{red}{3} + 1) - 2(\textcolor{red}{3}) + 3 = 13
$$

$$
4(4) - 6 + 3 = 13
$$

$$
16 - 6 + 3 = 13
$$

$$
13 = 13 \quad \checkmark
$$

Since both sides are equal, $x = 3$ is correct.


:::{.you-try title="Solve and check $3(x + 2) - x + 1 = 11$"}

**Step 1. Solve the equation**

$$
\begin{align*}
\textcolor{red}{3}(x + 2) - x + 1 &= 11 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{distribute the 3}}} \\
3x + 6 - x + 1 &= 11 \\
\\
\textcolor{blue}{3x} + \textcolor{green}{6} + \textcolor{blue}{-x} + \textcolor{green}{1} &= 11 \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{combine like terms}}} \\
\textcolor{blue}{2x} + \textcolor{green}{7} &= 11 \\
\\
2x + 7 \textcolor{red}{- 7} &= 11 \textcolor{red}{- 7} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{-7 both sides}}} \\
2x &= 4 \\
\\
2x \textcolor{red}{\div 2} &= 4 \textcolor{red}{\div 2} \tag*{\class{stepnote}{\textcolor{gray}{÷2 both sides}}} \\
x &= 2
\end{align*}
$$


**Step 2. Check the solution**

Substitute $x = 2$ into the **original equation**:

$$
\begin{align*}
3(x + 2) - x + 1 &= 11 \\
3(\textcolor{red}{2} + 2) - \textcolor{red}{2} + 1 &= 11 \\
3(4) - 2 + 1 &= 11 \\
12 - 2 + 1 &= 11 \\
11 &= 11 \quad \checkmark
\end{align*}
$$

:::
